name: Bias Checklist
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Before You Buy: A Working Checklist for Catching Your Own Biases
lesson.summary: A bias checklist turns the individual cognitive biases covered so far into a short, repeatable set of questions that can be run against any blockchain claim before acting on it.
lesson.body:
Knowing the name of a cognitive bias does surprisingly little, on its own, to prevent that bias from operating. Research on debiasing consistently finds that people are much better at spotting a given bias in someone else's reasoning than in their own, a pattern sometimes called the bias blind spot. A structured checklist compensates for this by turning bias awareness into a repeatable procedure, a short list of concrete questions run deliberately against a specific decision, rather than relying on remembering the right concept at the right moment under the emotional pressure of an actual investment decision.

A working checklist for evaluating a blockchain claim starts with the biases most relevant to how such claims get framed. Appeal to novelty: am I treating this project favorably mainly because it is new and exciting, without evidence it actually outperforms the alternative it claims to replace. Anchoring bias: is my sense of whether the current price is cheap or expensive being driven by a past price, such as an all time high, rather than by the asset's present fundamentals. Status quo bias: am I dismissing this proposal only because the existing system is familiar, or conversely, am I defending an existing crypto position only because changing my mind feels uncomfortable.

The checklist continues with three more established biases. Confirmation bias: have I mainly sought out information that supports a position I already hold, while giving less scrutiny to sources that challenge it. Sunk cost fallacy: am I holding onto or defending this position because of money or time I have already committed, rather than because of what the position is worth going forward, given that money and time already spent cannot be recovered by any future decision. Bandwagon effect: is a meaningful part of my confidence coming from the fact that many other people already believe or hold this, rather than from evidence I could describe if asked.

The checklist works best used explicitly and in writing, before a significant decision such as buying a token, following a project's roadmap claims, or dismissing a proposal outright, rather than as a vague mental habit. Writing down an honest answer to each question, even briefly, makes it harder to skip past an uncomfortable one. A yes answer to any item is not automatically a reason to abandon a position, biases can be present alongside a conclusion that is still correct, but it is a reliable signal that the position needs more independent evidence before it is trusted, and that the confidence behind it may be running ahead of what has actually been verified.

None of the individual biases on this list, and no checklist built from them, eliminates biased thinking entirely, since these are built in features of ordinary human cognition rather than defects that disappear once named. What a checklist changes is the odds: running through cognitive bias, confirmation bias, sunk cost fallacy, bandwagon effect, appeal to novelty, anchoring bias, and status quo bias as a fixed sequence, every time, catches a meaningful share of errors that would otherwise slip through unexamined. The next chapter places this checklist inside a broader critical thinking framework, one that covers not just which biases to check for, but how to reason through a claim from evidence to conclusion in the first place.
